name: Asher (son of Zilpah)
title: Ancestor of the tribe of Asher
summary: Asher was Silpah's second son and Jacob's eighth son, and became the ancestor of one of Israel's twelve tribes. His name is derived from the Hebrew word for 'happy' or 'blessed', and at his birth Leah exclaimed: "Happy am I! For women will call me happy." When Jacob on his deathbed blessed his sons, he prophesied that Asher's food would be rich and provide royal delicacies – a prophecy fulfilled when the tribe received one of Canaan's most fertile regions along the Mediterranean coast, from Carmel to Sidon, with abundant olive production. Moses confirmed this by saying that Asher should "dip his foot in oil". Despite the natural wealth of their territory, the tribe never fully drove out the Canaanites from their allotted cities, which shaped their religious and cultural development. The tribe's war history is mixed – Deborah's song criticizes them for passivity during the battle against Sisera. Nevertheless, Asher's descendants preserved their tribal identity through the centuries, well into New Testament times, where the prophetess Anna from the tribe of Asher recognized the child Jesus in the temple and testified that God's promises to Israel's tribes still stood firm.

keyEvents.title: The Birth of Asher
keyEvents.description: Asher was born as Zilpah's second son and Jacob's eighth son. Leah named him Asher and said: "Happy am I! For the women will call me happy."

keyEvents.title: The Journey to Egypt
keyEvents.description: Asher traveled with his father Jacob and the rest of the family to Egypt during the famine, to reunite with Joseph. His children are also mentioned here: the sons Jimna, Jishvah, Jishvi, and Beriah, as well as the daughter Serah.

keyEvents.title: Jacob's Blessing
keyEvents.description: On his deathbed, Jacob blessed his sons. Regarding Asher, he prophesied that his food would be rich and that he would provide royal delicacies.

keyEvents.title: Moses' Blessing over the Tribe of Asher
keyEvents.description: Moses blessed the tribe of Asher before his death and predicted that Asher would be blessed among the sons, find favor with his brothers, and dip his foot in oil. The strength of the tribe would last as long as they lived.

keyEvents.title: The Inheritance of the Tribe of Asher
keyEvents.description: The tribe of Asher was assigned a fertile territory along the Mediterranean coast in northern Canaan, from Mount Carmel toward Sidon, known for its olive trees and rich agricultural soil.

keyEvents.title: Canaanites Were Not Driven Out
keyEvents.description: The tribe of Asher failed to drive out the Canaanites from several of their allotted cities, including Acco, Sidon, and Achlab, and had to live among the original inhabitants.

keyEvents.title: Passivity during Deborah's War
keyEvents.description: In Deborah's song, the tribe of Asher is criticized for staying by the seashore and not joining the battle against the Canaanite commander Sisera.

versions.summary: Asher was the eighth son of Jacob, born to Zilpah, Leah's maidservant. His name means 'happy' or 'blessed,' and he became the ancestor of one of the twelve tribes of Israel. The tribe of Asher was known for its fertile land and abundant harvests.

versions.reason: [minor] Asher was not only a patriarch but also one of the twelve fathers of Israel. It is appropriate to add 'father' as a distinct role to clarify his function.; [major] According to Gen 46:17, Serah (Serach) is described as a daughter, not a son. It is important to clarify this. In addition, the name forms should be checked. Common Norwegian forms include Jimna, Jisjva, Jisjvi and Beria as sons, as well as Serah as a daughter.; [minor] The summary is good but could be expanded slightly to mention that Asher's tribe received land along the Mediterranean coast in northern Canaan, and that the prophetess Anna from Luke 2 belonged to the tribe of Asher – which provides a New Testament connection.; [minor] It may be worth noting that according to Judg 1:31-32, Asher's tribe did not drive out the Canaanites from several cities, which is an important event in the tribe's history.; [major] Footnotes are completely missing. Notes should be added regarding the etymology of the name, the geographical location of the tribe, and possibly the connection to the prophetess Anna in the NT.

versions.summary: Asher, the second son of Zilpah and Jacob's eighth son, received a name meaning 'happy' or 'blessed'. At his birth Leah exclaimed: "Happy am I! For women will call me happy." As ancestor of one of Israel's twelve tribes, Asher plays an important role in the unfolding of salvation history. On his deathbed Jacob prophesied that Asher's food would be rich and provide royal delicacies – a prediction fulfilled when the tribe received one of the most fertile regions in Canaan, along the Mediterranean coast from Carmel to Sidon, famous for its olive production. Moses repeated this blessing with words saying that Asher should "dip his foot in oil". Despite the natural abundance, the tribe was unable to completely drive out the Canaanites from their territory, which had lasting consequences. The tribe of Asher appears again in a New Testament context through the prophetess Anna, who recognized the child Jesus in the temple – a testimony that God's promises to the tribes were preserved through the centuries.

Although the patriarchs are credited with long lives, the most common estimate for Jacob's sons is somewhat shorter. However, this falls within a reasonable margin of uncertainty for the patriarchal period, and the chronology remains debated. Keep as it is.; [minor] In Gen 46:17, Heber and Malkiel, sons of Beriah, are also mentioned as descendants of Asher. The current list of five children (Jimnah, Ishvah, Ishvi, Beriah, Serah) is correct for direct children.; [minor] A reference could have been included to the participation (or lack thereof) of the tribe of Asher in Deborah's war, where the tribe is criticized for staying by the seashores (Judg 5:17). This is a well-known event associated with the tribe of Asher but is not critical to include.

footnotes.text: The name Asher (Hebrew: אָשֵׁר, ʾĀšēr) is derived from the root א-ש-ר, which means 'happy' or 'blessed.' At his birth, Leah exclaimed: "Happy am I!" (Gen 30:13). The same root appears in the Hebrew word 'ashrei,' which opens several psalms (e.g., Ps 1:1), expressing a deep state of divine blessing rather than fleeting happiness.

The territory of the tribe of Asher in northern Canaan, along the Mediterranean coast from Mount Carmel toward Sidon, was known for its fertility—especially olive cultivation. Moses' blessing that Asher would "dip his foot in oil" (Deut 33:24) reflects this. Archaeological finds in the region, including Iron Age olive presses, confirm extensive olive production in this area.

The prophetess Anna, who recognized the child Jesus in the temple (Luke 2:36–38), belonged to the tribe of Asher. This is one of very few New Testament references to the northern tribes and testifies that tribal identity was maintained even after the Assyrian deportation in 722 BC and the Babylonian exile.

According to rabbinic tradition (Bereshit Rabbah), the tribe of Asher was especially associated with abundance and wealth. The tradition tells that Asher's daughters were sought after as brides for priests and kings, partly due to the tribe's riches and the ritual significance of olive oil in anointing and purification ceremonies.

The tribe of Asher is mentioned among those tribes that failed to completely drive out the Canaanites from their allotted cities (Judg 1:31–32). The cities of Acco, Sidon, and Achzib remained under Canaanite control, which had long-lasting consequences for the tribe's religious integrity and cultural identity during the settlement period.

In Jacob's blessing (Gen 49:20), it is promised that Asher's "food shall be rich" and that he will "provide royal delicacies." The Hebrew word for 'rich' (שְׁמֵנָה, shemenah) is related to 'shemen' (oil), linking the blessing directly to the tribe's future olive production and underscoring the prophetic dimension of the patriarchs' statements.

In Deborah's song (Judg 5:17), the tribe of Asher is criticized for passivity during the war against Sisera: "Asher sat still at the seashore and remained by his harbors." This testifies to the tribe's close connection to coastal areas and port cities, but also to a tendency to prioritize trade and safety over the tribal confederation's shared military obligations.
